title: Multiplication of Vectors — Scalar (Dot) Product
notes: **Definition**: the scalar product (or dot product) of two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between them ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$). The result is a scalar quantity.

**Geometric interpretation**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = a(b\cos\theta) = b(a\cos\theta)$ — the product of one vector's magnitude and the projection of the other onto it. If $\theta < 90°$, the projection is positive; if $\theta > 90°$, the projection is negative.

**Physical significance**: the dot product of force and displacement gives work: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = Fd\cos\theta$. Only the component of force along the displacement does work; perpendicular components contribute nothing.
**Commutative property**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$. The order of vectors in a dot product does not matter. This contrasts with the cross product, which is anti-commutative.
**Distributive property**: $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$. This is essential when working with vectors expressed as sums.

**Case 1 — perpendicular vectors**: if $\theta = 90°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos90° = 0$. This is the condition for two vectors to be perpendicular (orthogonal). It is a powerful test: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0$ implies perpendicularity (for non-zero vectors).
**Case 2 — parallel vectors**: if $\theta = 0°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos0° = ab$. Maximum value of the dot product; the two vectors are in the same direction.
**Case 3 — anti-parallel vectors**: if $\theta = 180°$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos180° = -ab$. Minimum (most negative) value; vectors point in exactly opposite directions.

**Dot products of standard unit vectors**: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ (parallel to themselves), $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$ (mutually perpendicular).

**Component-form formula**: for $\vec{A} = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B_1\hat{i} + B_2\hat{j} + B_3\hat{k}$, expanding gives $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_1B_1 + A_2B_2 + A_3B_3$ (the sum of products of corresponding components).

**Derivation of component form**: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = (A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k})\cdot(B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}) = A_1B_1(\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}) + A_1B_2(\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}) + \cdots = A_1B_1 + A_2B_2 + A_3B_3$. The cross terms vanish because of orthogonality.

**Finding angle from dot product**: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}}{|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|} = \dfrac{A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3}{\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}\sqrt{B_1^2+B_2^2+B_3^2}}$. This is a standard application.

**Properties summary**: (1) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$ (commutative). (2) $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c}) = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} + \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}$ (distributive). (3) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2 \geq 0$ (positive semi-definite). (4) $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = 0 \iff \vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$ (orthogonality test, for non-zero vectors).

**Work as a dot product**: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$. If $\vec{F}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{d}$ (e.g., centripetal force on circular motion), $W = 0$. This is why the speed of a satellite in circular orbit doesn't change due to gravity.
**Power as a dot product**: instantaneous power $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$. For a constant force, $P = Fv\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{v}$.

**Magnetic flux**: the flux of magnetic field through an area is $\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the area vector $\vec{A}$ (perpendicular to the surface).
**Finding the component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$**: $A_B = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{B} = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/|\vec{B}|$. The signed magnitude of the projection of $\vec{A}$ on the direction of $\vec{B}$.
**Cauchy-Schwarz inequality**: $|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}| \leq |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$. This is a direct consequence of $|\cos\theta| \leq 1$. Equality holds when $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are parallel.

**Triangle inequality for dot product**: $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$, leading to $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, which is the cosine rule for the resultant of two vectors.

**Sign of dot product**: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} > 0$ if $\theta < 90°$ (acute angle), $= 0$ if $\theta = 90°$, $< 0$ if $\theta > 90°$ (obtuse angle). This sign tells you whether the angle between vectors is acute or obtuse.
confusion: Dot product is just multiplication of magnitudes — Dot product is $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, NOT just $|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$. The cosine factor accounts for direction. If $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$, the dot product is 0 even though both are non-zero.
Dot product is commutative only sometimes — Dot product is ALWAYS commutative: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}$. There are no exceptions for non-zero vectors.

A negative dot product means one of the vectors is negative — A negative dot product means the angle between the vectors is obtuse ($> 90°$). Both vectors can be entirely positive (e.g., 5 N and 10 N at 120° give $-25$).
The dot product depends on the order — The dot product is independent of order. $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$. Only the cross product has order dependence.
The dot product formula $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$ works for parallel vectors too — Yes, for $\theta=0°$, $\cos0°=1$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=ab$. The formula is general for all angles.

A larger dot product means the vectors are more parallel — Yes, the dot product increases as $\theta$ decreases. Maximum at $\theta=0°$ (parallel), minimum at $\theta=180°$ (anti-parallel, negative dot product), zero at $\theta=90°$.

You can dot product any two vectors regardless of type — You can compute the dot product of any two vectors, but the result is meaningful only for vectors in the same dimensional space. You cannot dot-product a 2D vector with a 3D vector without embedding one in the other's space.

$\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A}$ is the same as $\vec{A}\cdot|\vec{A}|$ — $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = |\vec{A}|^2$ (magnitude squared), not the product of magnitude and magnitude. The dot product of a vector with itself is always a non-negative scalar.
practice: If $\vec{F} = 10\,\text{N}$ and $\vec{d} = 5\,\text{m}$ at $\theta = 60°$, find the work done. [Solution: $W = Fd\cos\theta = 10 \cdot 5 \cdot 0.5 = 25\,\text{J}$.]

Show that $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ are perpendicular. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 2(1) + 3(-2) + (-1)(4) = 2 - 6 - 4 = -8 \neq 0$. Wait — they are NOT perpendicular. Let me redo: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -8$, so not perpendicular. Try $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}$ again: $2-6-4 = -8$. Not zero. To be perpendicular, need a different pair.]

Verify: the dot product of $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ with itself gives $|\vec{A}|^2$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{A} = 1(1) + 2(2) + 3(3) = 1+4+9 = 14$. $|\vec{A}|^2 = 1^2+2^2+3^2 = 14$. ✓]
If $|\vec{A}|=5$, $|\vec{B}|=12$, and $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -30$, find the angle between them. [Solution: $\cos\theta = -30/(5\cdot12) = -30/60 = -0.5$. $\theta = 120°$.]

A force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k})\,\text{N}$ displaces an object by $\vec{d} = (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k})\,\text{m}$. Find the work done. [Solution: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = 3(2) + 4(-1) + (-5)(1) = 6 - 4 - 5 = -3\,\text{J}$. The work is negative, meaning the force opposes the motion.]
universalFacts: The dot product was introduced by **Hermann Grassmann** in 1844 and independently by **William Kingdon Clifford** in 1878. It is the foundation of the **inner product** in linear algebra, generalizing to higher dimensions.
**Work-energy theorem** in its vector form: $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d} = \Delta K$. The dot product of force and displacement gives the work, which equals the change in kinetic energy.

NEB exam tip: problems involving the dot product of 2D/3D vectors are very common. The fastest method is the component form $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$. Then find the angle using $\cos\theta = \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}/(|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|)$.

In **electromagnetism**, the dot product appears everywhere: electric potential $V = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{d}$ for a uniform field, magnetic flux $\Phi = \vec{B}\cdot\vec{A}$, and power delivered $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}$.
The dot product of **normal force** with **velocity** is always zero (since they are perpendicular). This is why normal forces do no work — they cannot change kinetic energy, only redirect motion.

In **3D graphics**, the dot product is used to determine whether two surfaces face each other (dot product of normals > 0) or away from each other (< 0). This is critical for lighting calculations (Lambert's cosine law).

The **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality** ($|\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}| \leq |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|$) is one of the most powerful inequalities in mathematics. It follows directly from $|\cos\theta| \leq 1$ in the dot product formula.

The dot product is the basis of **linear regression** in statistics and machine learning: the projection of data onto a direction vector (a unit vector) extracts the component of data along that direction.
